query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of multi‐element, near‐equiatomic nanoparticles to retain structural and chemical stability at high operating temperatures is governed by the intrinsic sluggish atomic diffusion generated by high configurational entropy. This entropy‐driven suppression of atomic mobility prevents rapid elemental segregation and phase transformation. In contrast, introducing a minor dopant that disrupts this entropy (by causing local atomic size mismatch) should accelerate diffusion-driven instability.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized as uniformly mixed, single-phase solid solutions (near‐equiatomic composition) with high configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled dopant (or alter the atomic size distribution) that is predicted to lower the configurational entropy and reduce the sluggish diffusion effect while keeping the overall composition similar.
generation.conditions: Exposure to service regimes relevant for catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) applications under inert or reducing atmospheres to avoid extraneous oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The intrinsically slow atomic diffusion arising from high configurational entropy, which maintains a homogeneous elemental distribution and suppresses phase separation.
generation.mechanism: The high mixing entropy in near‐equiatomic nanoparticles inherently slows down atomic mobility, thus retarding segregation and phase transitions even under high temperature conditions. Disrupting this state (via dopant addition that introduces local chemical/size perturbations) is expected to increase diffusion rates, leading to faster onset of microstructural changes and chemical inhomogeneity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the same thermal conditions, the baseline (undoped) nanoparticles will maintain their single-phase structure and homogeneous elemental distribution over extended annealing times, whereas the doped nanoparticles will show accelerated onset of phase changes (e.g., formation of precipitates or segregation trends) and a decline in catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced without the dopant, which, thanks to their high configurational entropy, exhibit stable solid-solution behavior under specified service temperatures.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant in particles with equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions and in temperature regimes where diffusion kinetics are normally enhanced (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectrics). At very extreme temperatures, melting or sintering may introduce other degradation pathways.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative effect of the dopant on configurational entropy and the precise temperature thresholds where diffusion becomes significant remain uncertain and could depend on the nanoparticle size and exact compositional adjustments.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one set as the control (high-entropy, near-equiatomic solid solution) and a second set with a minor, deliberately chosen dopant designed to disrupt the uniform diffusion properties. Subject both sets to isothermal annealing at a representative temperature (e.g., 900 K for catalytic applications or 1500 K for thermoelectric testing) in an inert/reducing atmosphere. Monitor the evolution of the microstructure and compositional homogeneity over time.
measurements: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for observing phase transitions or segregation events
X-ray diffraction (XRD) for detecting phase changes
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping for assessing elemental distribution
Diffusion rate or degradation kinetics measurements via in-situ techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the baseline, undoped nanoparticles exhibit similar or greater rates of phase transformation, segregation, or degradation compared to the doped samples when subjected to the same thermal treatment. In other words, if the intervention does not produce a detectable acceleration of instability, then the role of sluggish diffusion (mediated by high entropy) in governing nanoparticle stability is not supported.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
